utterances.text: I went to my other aunt's house and we stayed there overnight. And in the night-time we were staying there. We had also candlelight there because there was no power whatsoever. We heard something and we thought: Oh my God, not again. We thought it was the police -- police officers, so we went kind of a huge hill and there were -- thought that I'm going to get hurt but I was fine on my own. My aunt -- my other aunt broke her leg, and by the time we knew it wasn't actual police officers and then we went back to the house, and we said: We have to get out of here first thing in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you leave the next day?

utterances.speaker: DREN CAKA
utterances.text: Yes. We got our things packed and we left.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who was in the group you went with?

utterances.speaker: DREN CAKA
utterances.text: My aunt, my uncle, my aunt's husband, my grandma and grandpa and my aunt's little daughter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How did you travel, by foot, in a car?

utterances.speaker: DREN CAKA
utterances.text: Me, my aunt, her husband and her daughter were in a car. My grandma and grandpa and uncle, they went by huge trucks which took people across the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: DREN CAKA
utterances.text: We went to Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know where you crossed?

utterances.speaker: DREN CAKA
utterances.text: In Kukes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Caka, I want to ask you about the men you described as police you saw that night. Since that time have you had a chance to look at some photographs of various uniforms?

utterances.speaker: DREN CAKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you recognise any of those as being similar to the ones you saw of the policemen wearing that night?

utterances.speaker: DREN CAKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to show the witness portions of Exhibit P2254, and I have a hard copy I'd like to hand him because I think it's easier for him to turn the pages by hand. And then if he can --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you recognise any photo, Mr. Cacak, will you tell us and then I can tell the court officer or the registry officer which page that would be in the e-court version of 2254.

utterances.speaker: DREN CAKA
utterances.text: For the jackets I saw photo 12, page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And I believe photo 12 would be on page 7 of the e-court.

utterances.speaker: DREN CAKA
utterances.text: This says page 6 at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. Could you wait just a minute. We're going to put that up on the screen and see if what's on the screen is the same thing that you're looking at in the hard copy. And you described it as photo number?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Any others?

utterances.speaker: DREN CAKA
utterances.text: At the bottom for the pants is -- I'm not too sure. It looks like the photo number 14 on the page 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. That would be the next page in the e-court version. Thank you. When you got to Kukes did you get any other further treatment for your injury, for your wound?

utterances.speaker: DREN CAKA
utterances.text: As soon as I crossed the border, like halfway between the Kosovo border and the Albanian border, as soon as I was halfway, help came to me. There was this Albanian guy. I think he was from Kosovo. He got a hold of me. They carried me. And then by the time I knew I was put to sleep, so for about four or five days there I don't remember anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's not very clear, Mr. Hannis, where that would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Where the border would be, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, halfway between the Kosovo border and the Albanian border. That doesn't make any sense to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you remember crossing the border on your way out of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: DREN CAKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In the car?

utterances.speaker: DREN CAKA
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall how far it was from that border crossing point to the hospital in Kukes where you went, or how long it took?

utterances.speaker: DREN CAKA
utterances.text: It took about ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now I want to ask you -- do you still suffer any effects from the bullet wound you received that day?

utterances.speaker: DREN CAKA
utterances.text: No, it's quite good. They asked me if I wanted to break it one more time because it's still not on right, but it's strong -- I play baseball, so it's fine now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you show the Judges where you were hit? Do you mind?

utterances.speaker: DREN CAKA
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you stand and show us on your arm where you received the wound.

utterances.speaker: DREN CAKA
utterances.text: That's it. [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You're indicating your right bicep. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, next, Your Honours, I would like to play a video that's Exhibit P2278. There's an accompanying transcript that's 2277. We have hard copies of the transcript available. The video is approximately two minutes and 20 seconds. And I don't know if it's helpful to the Court to have a hard copy to read along as the video is playing. Do you have hard copies, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I certainly was -- received one, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we're ready could we play the video. I don't know that we're getting any sound. Can the -- can the booth help us? I'm seeing a sign from the booth that they --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We'll give it another try here. I apologise, Your Honours. We're not getting any sound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you at the end of your examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm told to instruct you to release the video, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: To delete the video?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: To release the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: To release the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Our powers are limited to some extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: "We went into the house, the daughter of Lulzim Vejsa was chased by them with an automatic rifle, but they did not harm her, they only shot at the furniture, and the house started burning. "And then how did they get killed, did you see them? "And then we were made to sit on the couches. "They made you sit on the couches. "They killed Flaka Hoxha first. "Just a second. "Don't give him anything to eat at this moment. "It doesn't matter, it doesn't matter at all, Flaka's father was killed too. "No, the father is alive. "Grandfather, pardon me, grandfather, Flaka's grandfather was killed and her aunt, Muni. "No, Muni is alive. "Really? "Yes, he's alive. "How old was Flaka, Flaka Hoxha? "Did you see them killing Flaka? Did they shoot her with an automatic rifle? "Yes, with a machine-gun. "By a machine-gun, they shot ... "Did they shoot at their back? "Yes, and in their head. "How did they escape -- how did you escape? "He was wounded. "Those policemen were standing on the kitchen door ... I walked there slowly ... I was lying down, pretending to be dead, and when they left I went into the room, I almost choked from the smoke ... "And when they moved from the door, he run in another room was burning. It was the smoke, a lot of smoke inside. He stay on that smoke. "How long did you, Dren, sweetheart, how long did you stay in that room? "I think around half an hour. And they left the room and they left us as well, and then they left. "You shouldn't be afraid. No, honey, don't be afraid. Don't use the scissors. "She will only give it to you intravenously and you will fall asleep and nothing else. "I'm afraid that they will put me to sleep and then they will operate on me. "No, they are not going to operate on you in a tent. Where did you hear of a person having surgery in a tent, Dreni? "Please don't do anything to me with scissors."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Caka, have you seen that before?

utterances.speaker: DREN CAKA
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is that you?

utterances.speaker: DREN CAKA
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: There was another younger child pictured in that video for a portion. Do you know who that was? Oh, sorry. In the video there was another -- there was another child pictured. Do you know who that was that was in the tent with you.

utterances.speaker: DREN CAKA
utterances.text: I can't understand anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You're not getting any --

utterances.speaker: DREN CAKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You understand my English?

utterances.speaker: DREN CAKA
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you getting it now?

utterances.speaker: DREN CAKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In the video the camera panned to another injured child. Do you know who that was?

utterances.speaker: DREN CAKA
utterances.text: I don't recall his name, but he was another kid that there was a massacre and he had one side of his leg blown off. He was on the same helicopter as me, taking us from Kukes to Tirana. And there was no more -- the helicopter couldn't take any more people in. And my aunt asked his mother: What's your name, give me your address, I'll try care of him, and when I see you next time I'll try to look for you when we're back in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So that video was when you were in Kukes in the field hospital?

utterances.speaker: DREN CAKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Where were you taken from there?

utterances.speaker: DREN CAKA
utterances.text: To Tirana.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how long were you in Tirana?

utterances.speaker: DREN CAKA
utterances.text: About four or five months.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender the video 2278 and the transcript 2277.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Caka, of the 21 of you that were in the basement and then taken to the house that night, were you the only one to get out alive?

utterances.speaker: DREN CAKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have no more questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes. First it will be counsel for General Lukic and thereafter we'll follow the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Caka.

utterances.speaker: DREN CAKA
utterances.text: Hi.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm Branko Lukic, and I represent General Lukic together with my colleagues Mr. Ivetic and Mr. Ogrizovic. I just have a few questions for you, and I kindly ask you to help me just to clarify a few things you remember, or if you don't remember, just tell me and that's fine. Okay?

utterances.speaker: DREN CAKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We were -- we are pretty eager to know, and if you can help us with that, what is your neighbour's name that you described that took part in the killings of your family?

utterances.speaker: DREN CAKA
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you described those police officers in your statement from May the 12th, 2001, you said: "I saw three policemen. They wore blue camouflage uniforms. They had guns in holster pockets on their sides. They had greenish-coloured bullet-proof vests over their uniforms, and hanging from their vests they had many grenade bombs. They had big walkie-talkie radios, and I saw one policeman talk into the radio in Serb. They each carried a big rifle. Two of them wore hats. They wore knives and shields, at least one I saw in a shield on a policeman's leg." I know that you were young at that time, but would you agree with me that this is not a description of a regular police officer, was it not?

utterances.speaker: DREN CAKA
utterances.text: This is not -- no, it's not. But there weren't any -- there weren't any green vests. There was all blue and blue camouflage. And there was no bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So this description we have in front of us is not hundred per cent accurate?

utterances.speaker: DREN CAKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do they -- had -- did they have hats in their --

utterances.speaker: DREN CAKA
utterances.text: One of them had a hat.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And how did those big guns look like, they --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: AK-47, okay. And can you remember any more details regarding their uniforms? Have you seen any badges?

utterances.speaker: DREN CAKA
utterances.text: No, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, is that statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll tell you. It's -- I can refer to the exact paragraph. It's the statement from the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but does it have a P number?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- 2001 -- I was informed that there is no P number to this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you haven't introduced it into the e-court library?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, we haven't, Your Honour. But I think that I got the clarification I seeked for it, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you don't seek to do so?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If it's not too late, I would like to have it introduced, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have no objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I -- I think what you ought to do is have it introduced into the system and then tomorrow you can tell me what number it has.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It would be 6D69.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It is -- all right, well, we'll note it's 6D69 and leave it to you to introduce it into the system.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Caka, in this case the Prosecutor interviewed one protected witness with a pseudonym K74, and in his statement on the page 3, paragraph 6, he claims that in that attack, among other attackers, there was some Albanians. Did you by any chance recognise anybody among those people as being an Albanian?

utterances.speaker: DREN CAKA
utterances.text: The police officers?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: DREN CAKA
utterances.text: There weren't any Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You told us that some of these police officers spoke Albanian?

utterances.speaker: DREN CAKA
utterances.text: They spoke -- they only said: Are you guys with the Albanian army? And we said: No, we're just -- we want to be in a safe place.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. So you haven't recognised anybody from Jakupi family?

utterances.speaker: DREN CAKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, do you know who's meant by the Jakupi family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Although you cannot give us the exact name of this neighbour of yours, do you still remember how did he look like? Can you give us more details about his appearance?

utterances.speaker: DREN CAKA
utterances.text: He had hair. He's the one that was right by the windows, and he -- he had about short brownish hair and dark eyes, dark -- probably dark brown eyes and about -- height around 180, and weight, had a stomach a little bit. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember anything specific regarding his uniform?

utterances.speaker: DREN CAKA
utterances.text: No. They were all the same uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. You described to us your trip to the hospital. Was it a regular hospital? Walk-in clinic? Emergency? If you can remember.

utterances.speaker: DREN CAKA
utterances.text: In Kukes?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: DREN CAKA
utterances.text: It was the regular hospital where it still is right now. And we walked -- we walked in right afterwards and -- like I said before, we walked in the hospital. There was one Serbian soldier there and he said: What happened? And my grandfather told him. And he says: Oh, I feel bad. We shouldn't be harming women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In -- do you remember in which language have you spoken with that medical personnel, doctor or a nurse?

utterances.speaker: DREN CAKA
utterances.text: The doctor, he was Albanian, but the soldier -- the soldier who was there, he was Serbian but can speak Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And do you remember whether any record was made at that time regarding your injury?

utterances.speaker: DREN CAKA
utterances.text: No. I was right in and out of there. Just took an X-ray. They said my arm was broken, but I already knew that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Caka. I don't have any more questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic -- oh, sorry, Mr. Ackerman. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: One maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: With regard to the neighbour who you said was a policeman, do you recall indicating a name in 1999 when you were interviewed about this?

utterances.speaker: DREN CAKA
utterances.text: I probably gave the name, but now I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In your statement it mentions the name Novica, Gjoka's son, does that ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: DREN CAKA
utterances.text: [No verbal response].

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was the answer to that? No. Well, it says "no verbal response." What was your answer to that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You don't remember, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Caka, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give your evidence. You're now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Oh, I see Mr. Lukic is up, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Wisdom first.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: -- introduce a very rare moment of levity into the trial. I didn't think it would be appropriate with the witness here, but I'd love to come back at a time 43 years from now when I'm no longer around, but I'd love to come back when he's aged 60 and ask him if he still thinks that 60 is an old man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Like everything else, Mr. Sepenuk, age is relative. The elderly Mr. Lukic is anxious to address us as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I don't think that I will be that charming as Mr. Sepenuk, because I have one problem to raise. You also mentioned today, before, that we have to limit our cross-examinations, but I can assure you that a lot of our cross-examinations arise from the additions to the witness statements, as we have with the next witness. I was sure yesterday that I would be one day to rest at least, not having to cross this witness, but then we received the supplemental statement in which this witness connects, unlike before, police and paramilitary. So now I have to go with him through the whole of his statement and every single one. So we -- and it wasn't disclosed and we object to admission. I know that even the Prosecutor -- Prosecutor didn't propose the admission of this document, but it might be proposed by one of my colleagues who defend military. Now, I would have been in the position to jump again and to object and to at the end cross-examine this witness. So if we want to have a mess of this case, then we can continue this way. But what if the Defence continues with the same practice, if we provide the other side with the 65 ter statements from our witnesses and change it on a day of the direct examination? I think that it's not all right to proceed with this kind of practice. And I apologise for taking your time, Your Honours, but we really have -- we have -- I think that Your Honours should give some guidelines to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is not something to apologise for because on the face of it it's a -- on the face of it, I haven't heard the answer yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On the face of it, what you're saying sounds very reasonable.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So let's hear what Mr. Hannis has to say in response. Mr. Stamp then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. I caught the last part of the submission by my learned friend --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you can read it -- I'll give you a moment to read it on the screen there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lukic, what you must be referring to is something that has not come the way of the Trial Chamber yet. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honours, whether you received this, but it's the addendum from 27th of August, 2006 -- statement actually, statement, from 27th of August, 2006. And it hasn't been tendered by the Prosecution, so maybe you don't have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If it's not in fact being presented as a statement, then are you able to identify for me where you claim that you've not been given adequate notice of the line of evidence that is to be followed?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I anticipate that this document might be tendered, as I told you, by my other colleagues because they might use it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And this part which bothers me is not part of 65 ter statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The trouble is -- this is one of these problems that I -- that is not soluble, so I understand your approach now, that you would be taking a stricter line if it was simply material which supported the Prosecution case. What you fear is that other accused can use this material produced so late and you realise it's difficult for you to oppose that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Or the Prosecution might lead the evidence on it. We don't know yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed, but -- yeah. I think I need to be clear about the extent to which it's not heralded in the 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There is no any kind of mentioning of the connection in between police and the paramilitaries. Now we have those two groups interlinked completely by paragraph 2 of this new statement, only by one paragraph it applies on every single mentioning of the paramilitaries in his previous statements and probably today in his -- during his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you saying the previous testimony makes no mention of the police at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It does mention police but not in connection with paramilitaries. In one paragraph police was helping to find somebody's parents or I don't know, there is mentioning of police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But not adverse to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, not adverse to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. Just for clarification, may I first indicate that the additional statement -- the addendum to the previous statement was put into e-court as P2280 [Realtime transcript read in error "P2284"], and we transmitted it to the Defence in English and thereafter in B/C/S as soon as that became available. We did so as a matter of urgency because we realised that upon being asked in proofing certain questions about the evidence that it -- that he was to give, he said or gave information that he thought should be brought before the Court, and the Defence of course should be given notice of it. The mentioning of the police in conjunction with the paramilitaries shows to some extent it is considered to go beyond the 65 ter summary because the summary does not explicitly mention the police as being -- cooperating in this way with the paramilitaries, and in those circumstances we would seek the Court's leave to -- to amend the 65 ter summary and to proceed with the evidence as the witness is able to give it and as indicated -- or as notified to the Defence at the earliest opportunity when it became available -- when we became aware that the witness was in a position to say this. The number of the document, the addendum is 2280.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, you said 2284 a moment ago. Is it --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It is 2280.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: May I confuse the matter further, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I need a moment to read this, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lukic, is the direct reference confined to paragraph 2 and paragraph 9?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me check paragraph 9, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Maybe --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, in this paragraph he specifically mentions the police for the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What about paragraph 13, is that new as well, the second -- third sentence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, for the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wanted to point out that at 7.28 last night, at least I was sent and I suspect all my colleagues were sent a new 65 ter summary. And it did not include this new information, which in many ways tell you that they didn't intend to use it, otherwise they'd have put it in there. So that's -- I think that tends to cancel out the proposition that they notified us as soon as possible. They told us last night and the fact that they weren't going to use it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, in the new 65 ter summary can you show me where it implicates the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The 65 ter summary sent in the notification is the same 65 ter summary as was originally sent. The policy of the Prosecution is that we would not change the summaries without applying to the Court. The notification is the notification we give when we serve the Defence with the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Right. Well, I have lying on my desk two documents which I received today.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which are called: Updated 65 ter summaries. Why are they called updated if they are the same?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It seems, Your Honour, that in light of recent developments there is now developing a practice to do it that way. The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, this is chaos, isn't it --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Whoa, whoa. This is chaos. This case started -- was first investigated in 1999. I have, a number of times, outwith as well as inside the court made the comment that there is a time for investigating cases, and it's the pre-trial stage, at the very latest. And things should have been put in order in time to give everybody a reasonable opportunity to plan how they're going to conduct their part of the case, bearing in mind that there are going to have to be limitations placed on the parties' freedom to present the case at will. And this sort of thing is simply making it more and more difficult to manage the case. Now, this one's a particularly difficult one because I don't think there's a great deal involved on the face of it, but it has changed the complexion of who this witness will suggest is responsible for part of the conduct referred to in the statement and prior evidence. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed. The -- of course we accept that. The difficulty, of course, is if and when the witness comes for proofing and he's asked specific questions and he gives specific answers which are relative and probative of the issues before the Court, I think the Prosecution ought at least to apply to the Court to have it heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you see, I ask again the question: Why are these witnesses being proofed at this stage? It seems utterly ridiculous to me to wait until they're at the door of the court before a lawyer sits down with them and addresses their evidence; that's a lawyer with an understanding of the case as a whole. Because all that's going to happen is we're going to limp from witness to witness, unsure of what that witness's evidence is going to be until they come to court. Now, that's not -- that's not a good enough way to present an international case which is constantly in the public limelight. Are you short of money to carry out investigations at the right stage? Is that the problem? If so, then it should be out in the open.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is -- well, that is not something I'm able to address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, dear. Well, so you can't tell me the reason?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The -- but of course there are practical, logistical limitations on the amounts of time that we can approach or bring the witnesses here. Even the witnesses themselves resist coming here for long periods before they testify, and of course if we have them here for long periods, there are of course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the problem about lawyers going to Kosovo and actually investigating the case properly in the pre-trial phase at the latest? What's the problem there? Is it not cheaper for a lawyer to go there than to bring witnesses and all their accompanying personnel to The Hague? Anyway, we have to deal with this particular problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I make one remark here in connection with that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You'll recall in the pre-trial stage at one point we had 80 or 90, 92 bis witnesses who we had proposed as 92 bis without cross-examination. And that at that time we thought that might happen, or at least for a portion of them. We understand your decision and we don't disagree with it, but that was one reason that those people weren't seen. But the other is a practical, logistical resource problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, can I say that the first reason strikes me as extraordinarily naive because one thing that's absolutely clear from the way in which this case has been conducted so far is that there could have been the grossest miscarriage of justice if these witnesses had not been available for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand your point. But I indicate to you it's not naive on my part based on the experience in the other case that I worked on in the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, all that's happened through -- well, one thing that's become clear through cross-examination is that it was necessary. I shudder to think what might well have happened without that opportunity being available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, does it make any difference to your position if the hearing of this evidence is postponed at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can tell you our preference is first. We would kindly ask Your Honours to bar this kind of evidence to be introduced because it's after all time-limits introduced --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The problem about that in this case, and it may -- it may happen again, is that it's quite different from the evidence that we previously refused to hear because it was a discrete topic that could be separated from the rest of the witness's evidence. What we face here is evidence which is an expansion, elaboration, qualification, call it what you will, of the account previously given. So it's intertwined with the evidence given. Now, we have in mind the possibility that if this were to happen again and we couldn't easily separate the new evidence from the old, that we might refuse to hear the witness at all because it would be unrealistic to do anything else. But in relation to this witness, it's not clear that that's the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I could - I don't know if it's right time or not - direct you to the Milosevic transcript when she [sic] was particularly asked about paramilitaries, she never mentioned like this, said anything like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I think that's something that here you're going to be able to deal with by way of cross-examination. So my initial question at the moment is whether delay makes any difference or your point is a different one. It's just means that you have to spend time with the witness that you didn't envisage spending.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Of course that I would spend some time that I hadn't envisaged before. But still we would ask for this part at least, if not the whole, testimony of this witness be barred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You can see how unrealistic that is, Mr. Lukic. To exclude the witness entirely is feasible, but to exclude parts of the evidence is not. That's -- that's our problem. Anyway, we -- I've heard what you've said. We have ourselves discussed how we might proceed here. Now, Mr. Stamp, is -- just hold on a second. Is there another witness readily available?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we're also clear in our minds that -- we're also quite clear in our minds that if you seek relief in the form of additional time with the re-calling of the witness or whatever, then obviously we would view that sympathetically in a situation like the present. And we are prepared, to make it clear, that if this is repeated, then there is a distinct possibility of us refusing to hear the witness at all if we cannot separate out the bits of the evidence that are really new, in the sense that they are significant enough to bring an accused into the picture who was previously not in the frame. But in relation to this witness, I think we should hear that evidence and your cross-examination, for which there obviously will be a very strong foundation from the previous transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At least if we can get break after the direct examination so we can prepare ourselves further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, if you need that, you can raise it at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Stamp, in the rather exceptional circumstances here where there is a witness who can give evidence in line with a 65 ter summary but it emerges that there may be significant, though brief, parts of that evidence that are affected by new discoveries, we are -- and where no particular indication has been given before of the sort of action we might take when faced with a similar problem, we are prepared to allow the amendment of the 65 ter notification to demonstrate that this witness will speak -- will give evidence that would implicate the police. And we shall allow her -- him to testify on that basis. However, we make it clear now that there is a distinct possibility should this situation arise again, and we cannot simply exclude, easily exclude the additional evidence, then we would refuse to hear the witness because it would be unrealistic to do other than take that action if we are to keep this trial moving at a reasonable pace, as is inevitably required by the volume of material that parties seek to place before us. So you can now bring in the witness and we'll proceed to hear that evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I should have indicated also that in the notification we have indicated -- or we have made a cross-reference to the exhibits used in Milosevic that are -- in the Milosevic case that are of relevance here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Shabani.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you -- one second. Would you please now make the solemn declaration by reading aloud the document which is before you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Now, Mr. Shabani, we have before us written material containing evidence you have given and statements you have given, so we know a lot already about your account of events. The purpose of this hearing is to enable counsel for the parties to ask further questions for a number of reasons. They may be to clarify, they may be to allow you to give additional information, and they may be to challenge the evidence. Don't be surprised if questions are asked that appear to challenge your version of events because it is the job of lawyers in this system to ask that sort of question. That's the system under which this Tribunal operates. The first person to ask you questions will be on behalf of the Prosecution. Please listen carefully to the questions and try to limit your answer to the particular point that the question is directed to. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sir, could you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes, my name is Qamil Shabani.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Shabani, I see from here that you have something looking like notes. I -- I'm going to ask you to close them and just help us as much as you can from your memory. And if you need to refer to your notes you could ask His Honour, the President, for permission to do so. Thank you. Mr. Shabani, as His Honour indicated, we have already your statements and a transcript of your evidence which you gave before. But just for the record, did you give a statement to officers of the OTP at your home in the Zhegra village in June 2001?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And thereafter on the 4th of March, 2002, and the 6th of March, 2002, you attended here, testifying in the trial of Slobodan Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And following that, before you came here to testify on this occasion, did you on the 27th of August give some additional information to officers of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes, I gave some supplementary evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honours, that -- those three documents are in e-court as P02263 for the witness statement of June 2001; P02264 for the transcript in the case number IT-02-54; and P2280 for the recent addendum of the 28th -- 27th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I was indicating, Your Honour, just for the benefit of the Court, that we have in order to assist the Court in following the Milosevic transcript, indicated what the P numbers are for the evidence referred to in that case. There are different numbers. So one could cross-refer to the P numbers if one wishes to look at the document that the witness is referring to in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Shabani, you -- in your statement you indicated that you are from Zhegra village?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I am from Zhegra village.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Prior to March 1999, how long had you lived there?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: We have always lived in Zhegra, ever since we were born. Our fathers and forefathers have been living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you say "we." Did your family also live in Zhegra village?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes, yes. My family, too, lived in that village, and our ancestors lived there. We are ancient inhabitants of that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, you abandoned your village on the 29th of March, 1999, and went with your family and other villagers to the village of Stublla. Can you briefly in your own words tell us why you left your village?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: We left our village because of the Serb reprisals in the village against other inhabitants during the time that the NATO air bomb -- air-strikes started. Before that time, there were Serb police and army, two, three weeks before the strikes. Then other supplementary forces came and were stationed in the village on the 28th. And then they started the operations of cleansing the village from the Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can I stop you there. You said on the 28th they started the operations of cleaning the village of the Albanians. You said in your statement, and this is the third full paragraph of page 3 of the English version, and the second full paragraph of page 3 of the B/C/S version, that the soldiers started to expel people from the entrance of the building. How did you become aware of that? Did you actually observe this or were you told that?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. Can you repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. You just spoke of operations to clean the village of Albanians, and I'm referring you now to a part of your statement in which you said: "The next morning, the 23rd [sic] of March, 1999, the soldiers started to expel people from the entrance to the village. They went to the houses and forced the people to leave, ordering them with guns to leave the village. They started to shoot and frighten the people." How did you become aware that this was happening? Is this something you personally observed or were you told this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the date won't help, I think, because the date is the 29th of March, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The next morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is the 29th of March, yes, that's right, the 29th. The 29th of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So now that we've got that clear, you're being asked how you knew what was happening.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were there, in the village. And people were fleeing the village out of -- Serb forces who had entered their houses and looking for the most prominent figures in our village. They had pre-arranged lists with the help of the local Serbs. And they knew who the leaders of the political parties in Zhegra were. They were looking for the chairman of the LDK, Tahir Tahiri was his name, and other persons who had an influence in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. I thank you. Remember that we have our statement and the transcript of your testimony, so I'm just going to ask you to focus on one part of the question. The expulsion that you speak of on the morning of -- well, on the 29th of March, the morning in fact, how did you know that the soldiers were going about? You say you were there. Did you actually see the soldiers who were involved in the expulsion?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes, I saw them, and I heard them. It was because of them that I myself was forced to leave. They shelled the village with all sorts of weapons. They used APCs, machine-guns, and we could see them driving around the village. They shot at our houses, and they entered the houses of the local inhabitants and drove the inhabitants out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: So ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In your statement you said that you left the village and went to a hill called Kushlevica where you spent the night, and then you returned to the village and the next morning there was still shooting, and it was coming from the APCs that were driving through the village. Can you say whose -- what the APC is, firstly, and whose -- or which organisation did it belong to?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: It's an armoured car, and they belonged to the army, to the Serbian army, that was in the village at that time. And they were operating in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, I --

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: They shelled the houses of Albanians. That's why they were obliged to flee. As a result of that action, two persons got injured. One woman got injured on her right arm, and another person, a male, was wounded in his leg.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you went to the village of -- and I may get the pronunciation wrong, I had it written - anyway, Stublla?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. About how many other villagers went there with you?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: We were around 1300 people, all from that part of the village that was on the side of the river that runs through the village. So the village is divided in two parts. We were about 1.300 villagers who went in the direction of Stublla. We spent the night there and then we -- the next day we returned to Zhegra. But in the morning of the 29th, the Serbian forces started to fire again at the village and its population. And in the house of Tahir Tahiri, who was the chairman of the LDK branch who they wanted liquidate.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: They killed his brother, Shyqri Tahiri.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thanks. That is in your statement. When you left your village to stay in Stublla for five weeks, what date was that?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: It was the 29th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And from there you eventually went to Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes. We stayed in Stublla for five weeks, and then after five weeks we went to Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you give us an number, just an approximate number, about how many refugees from Kosovo went with you or in your group to Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: In our group, yes, initially we were around 600 people. Then other -- then 60 other people from Isufaj village joined us. And then when we approached the border, another 300 joined our group that went to Macedonia. These happened later, at the stage when we started to go to Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you think you would be able to mark on a map the route you took from your village to Stublla and from Stublla to Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes, I can do that. I can also do that for other groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown map P36. May I just indicate to the Court that although that was dealt with in the previous trial, he just made indications apparently, so there were no markings on the exhibit. So the exhibit from that case would not be helpful here. Can you just pan it in so that we can read the place names, please. Can you zoom in, please -- oh, sorry. Thank you. That's good. Thank you very much. I think you probably need to zoom out just a little bit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please enlarge it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think it would be helpful if you could move the centre of the map further to the top of the map, to scroll down, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just a minute, just a minute. Can you see on that map Gnjilane?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you see your hometown, your home village, Zhegra?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes, it's here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you put a circle -- oh, dear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You need to zoom out. Would it be able to mark a hard copy on the ELMO? I think we'll be able to move more quickly. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Shabani, go to your left. Look to the document on your left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Shabani, the document is on your left. Now, first identify where your village is on that map, and then put a circle around it.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: It's here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And could you next identify where Stublla is, the village that you sought refuge first?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And could you just quickly mark the route from your village to Stublla and then from Stublla across the border to Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just, if you can, draw a line along the route.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you see on the map where the border crossing was? Can you put an X where the border crossing was, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters don't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you put an X there.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. And ...

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. I think ...

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. How did you travel from Zhegra to Stublla?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: We walked on foot. The entire population walked all the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And from Stublla to Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: From Stublla to Macedonia, we walked, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'd like to take you through one or two documents very quickly, if you can help me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit P1325. And while that is being done, could that map be given an exhibit number as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That depends on whether the registrar can multi-task.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this map will be given the exhibit number IC27.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I will, for brevity, lead the witness straight through this part of evidence because this was testified in Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said earlier or -- in the previous occasion that you testified here that the photos number 6 --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we move on to photo number 6, 7, and 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- Were some of the vehicles that the army possessed in the vicinity of Zhegra shortly before you had to abandon your -- the village. Do you see them? Do you see those vehicles 6, 7, and 8 in front of you?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes, I do. And all these that I see here were part of the vehicles I saw in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, you said -- you also said in your statement that there was a -- an APC, a military APC, that fired on the village's house -- houses. Do you see it here?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: [No verbal response].

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you recall which one it was? Sorry, do you see it here. You didn't answer verbally. Could you answer orally, please, for the record.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, there was such a vehicle, and there were -- it was open on top and there were soldiers standing there, and it was an armoured car.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The one that you say you saw driving through Zhegra and firing on the houses; do you see there?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: In this screen I don't see that vehicle, but the other ones that I see here were also seen in the village. Maybe it's in another part of the screen, the one you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we go back to the first page of this exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And what I'm trying to ask you to identify if you can or to tell us if you can is if you see the vehicle that drove through Zhegra firing at the houses.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: I don't find it here. It's armoured, but it's open, as I said, on top. I could see soldiers standing there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we move to Exhibit P1326.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is that -- is that document clear to you? Can you see it clearly?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said that you saw soldiers in the vicinity of your village. Do you see any of the uniforms that they wore while they were there in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes. Here, in this picture. In this picture below.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which number is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nine.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you see any others?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I can make out the numbers, so could you just put a dot or a mark on the number 6, please. Just mark it. If you can mark number 6, please, the one you call number 6, because I can't see the numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You must get your screen seen to, then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thanks. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: There were also reservists, militia, and they had this kind of uniform resembling the police uniform, but they were reservists. I saw such-like in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Which uniform is that? Are you still referring to number 6?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: This uniform here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Touch the number, please.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Number 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Obviously this isn't as quick as you thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So we'll need to break. We're already ten minutes past the time. I thought you were finishing --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I was, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that you finished?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I am not finished, but I was finishing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, no, we'll break now, then, and we'll resume at 6.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. The Prosecution would have no further questions at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When you said earlier that you were relating certain exhibits to their Milosevic transcript references, is that confined to the two that we've just looked at?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Or is there some place that you say there is a cross-reference?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Oh, there is in the witness notification. I thought I -- I probably did not. In the column description of the exhibits, there is a cross-reference to the Milosevic transcript page number and exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The order will be: General Pavkovic, General Ojdanic, General Lazarevic, General Lukic, Mr. Sainovic, and Mr. Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, my colleagues have asked me to, on their behalf, respectfully request of Your Honours that we defer cross-examination until 9.00 tomorrow morning because of the matter that was -- that came up very recently.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you have any comment to make on this, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- just say that it is indeed a difficult position where these new matters arise. There's no gain saying that. However, I think a practical review of what the new matter -- material is by counsel may enable them to at least proceed today and finish tomorrow. When I say that, I in no way try to lighten the impact of the concession I do make, that these late revelations are -- present difficulties and are unfortunate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One way of dealing with this if it is to be a regular problem might be for us to make an order that any additional 65 ter notification has to be made one month in advance of the witness giving evidence. What would your response to that be?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Immediately I could say that that would be a very, very difficult situation for the Prosecution. The Prosecution would probably have to forego leading new information in that case. In many situations, I think we would only in very limited circumstances be able to -- and a very limited number of witnesses be able to make that type of expedition to get that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the Chamber are satisfied that the request made in the circumstances is a reasonable one and will grant it and will hold the time lost against the Prosecution in the circumstances. It's coming that the -- the date is coming closer when we're going to have to look at the management of time again, and this may be a relevant factor in our consideration of that issue. Mr. Shabani, I'm sorry that this has happened, but as a result of developments over which we have no control, the -- it's not possible to proceed further today with the case and it will have to be adjourned until tomorrow. You're required to come back here to continue your evidence at 9.00 tomorrow morning. Meanwhile, it's very important that you do not have any discussion with anyone at all about your evidence, that's either the evidence you've given or the evidence you've yet to give. You can talk about anything else except the evidence. And tomorrow we will not sit later than 1.30 and possibly -- well, we'll finish as conveniently as is possible shortly before 1.30, but 1.30 is a deadline tomorrow. So 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 1st day of September, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.22 p.m.,
